Evolving Jailbreaks: Automated Multi-Objective Long-Tail Attacks on Large Language Models

Wenjing Hong Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: Shenzhen Univeristy, China Email: hongwj@szu.edu.cn    Zhonghua Rong Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: Shenzhen Univeristy, China Email: 2410673015@mails.szu.edu.cn    Li Wang Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: Shenzhen Univeristy, China Email: wangli100@szu.edu.cn    Feng Chang Affiliation: Brain-Inspired Technology Co.,Ltd, China Email: changfeng@leinao.ai    Jian Zhu Affiliation: Brain-Inspired Technology Co.,Ltd, China Email: Zhujian@leinao.ai    Ke Tang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology, China Email: tangk3@sustech.edu.cn    Zexuan Zhu ††thanks: corresponding author Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: Shenzhen Univeristy, China Email: zhuzx@szu.edu.cn    Yew-Soon Ong Affiliation: College of Computing & Data Science Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore Email: asysong@ntu.edu.sg
Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely deployed, especially through free Web-based applications that expose them to diverse user-generated inputs, including those from long-tail distributions such as low-resource languages and encrypted private data. This open-ended exposure increases the risk of jailbreak attacks that undermine model safety alignment. While recent studies have shown that leveraging long-tail distributions can facilitate such jailbreaks, existing approaches largely rely on handcrafted rules, limiting the systematic evaluation of these security and privacy vulnerabilities. In this work, we present EvoJail, an automated framework for discovering long-tail distribution attacks via multi-objective evolutionary search. EvoJail formulates long-tail attack prompt generation as a multi-objective optimization problem that jointly maximizes attack effectiveness and minimizes output perplexity, and introduces a semantic-algorithmic solution representation to capture both high-level semantic intent and low-level structural transformations of encryption-decryption logic. Building upon this representation, EvoJail integrates LLM-assisted operators into a multi-objective evolutionary framework, enabling adaptive and semantically informed mutation and crossover for efficiently exploring a highly structured and open-ended search space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EvoJail consistently discovers diverse and effective long-tail jailbreak strategies, achieving competitive performance with existing methods in both individual and ensemble level.

   

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in natural language processing and are increasingly deployed through Web platforms, powering search engines [43], chat interfaces [28], social media [31], and other online applications. These Web-mediated deployments enable unprecedented research opportunities, such as large-scale behavioral studies and real-time data collection [4]. At the same time, they expose critical security and privacy risks, as the generation of harmful or unsafe content can compromise user safety and erode the integrity of the Web ecosystem [39]. Existing safeguards mitigate some risks but remain far from foolproof, making systematic evaluation of LLM vulnerabilities a pressing need for model developers, Web platform operators, and the broader AI safety community [24, 42, 33].

Jailbreak attacks have emerged as a key methodology for probing LLM safety in Web-facing applications, by inducing models to bypass alignment mechanisms and produce otherwise restricted outputs [47]. Such attacks reveal vulnerabilities that could be exploited in online environments and prior research has explored various strategies such as rule-based strategies [1], greedy coordinate gradient [53, 16], optimization [20, 3], psychological weaknesses exploitation [44]. However, most existing approaches rely on conventional natural language patterns, whereas real-world Web environments expose LLMs to diverse, user-generated inputs that often deviate from such distributions.

Recently, a growing line of research has focused on exploiting long-tail distributions to bypass safety alignment [35]. This is achieved by crafting inputs that deviate substantially from the training distribution and are often unintelligible to humans, yet retain latent semantic representations that cause models to produce harmful or policy-violating outputs. A number of studies has been proposed to explore such inputs from long-tail distributions, including low-resource or multilingual jailbreaks [6], cryptographically encoded or code-style prompts [48, 23, 15], noise-induced mode flipping [21], symbol-level perturbations [14], and tokenization vulnerabilities [9].

Despite these advances, most long-tail distribution attacks remain depend on expert-crafted rules or templates, requiring extensive manual effort. In contrast, the observation of the above diverse existing strategies highlights the vast and highly non-uniform nature of the adversarial prompt space and underscores the need for systematic exploration. These limitations hinder the development of automated, generalizable jailbreak frameworks, which are crucial for ensuring the security of LLMs in practical Web contexts.

To address these challenges, this paper presents EvoJail, an automated framework for discovering long-tail distribution attacks via multi-objective evolutionary search that jointly optimizes attack effectiveness and output quality. At its core, EvoJail introduces a semantic-algorithmic representation in which candidate solutions are explicitly modeled as reversible encryption-decryption algorithm pairs, enabling the simultaneous manipulation of high-level semantics and low-level structural transformations. To efficiently explore the resulting highly discrete and structured search space, EvoJail integrates LLM-assisted initialization, mutation, crossover and repair operators into a unified multi-objective evolutionary loop, where evolutionary feedback is explicitly incorporated to guide adaptive and semantically informed variation. The main contribution of this paper is summarized as follows.

  1. 1)

    The EvoJail method is introduced as the first automated framework that leverages inputs from long-tail distributions to attack LLMs via multi-objective evolutionary search. It eliminates the reliance on handcrafted rules and enables systematic evaluation of security and privacy vulnerabilities across diverse user-generated inputs exposed by real-world Web environment.

  2. 2)

    The framework constructs the search space by combining semantic information and algorithmic descriptions, and incorporates LLM-assisted operators to enhance the search process. This design allows the algorithm to efficiently explore the encryption-decryption prompt space while providing adaptive and interpretable attack strategies.

  3. 3)

    Extensive experiments demonstrate that EvoJail achieves competitive performance in both attack effectiveness and output quality while producing a diverse Pareto front of attack strategies. This diversity is essential for supporting flexible and adaptive attack strategies in different evaluation scenarios.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on evolutionary optimization for jailbreak attacks and long-tail distribution attacks. Section III presents the proposed EvoJail framework in detail, including the problem formulation, evolutionary operators, and overall optimization procedure. Section IV reports and analyzes the experimental results. Finally, Section V concludes the paper and discusses potential directions for future research.

2 Related Works

2.1 Evolutionary Jailbreak Attacks

Evolutionary algorithms have recently been explored as powerful black-box strategies for generating adversarial prompts against LLMs. AutoDAN [19] employs a hierarchical genetic algorithm, while AutoDAN-Turbo [20] extends this approach with a lifelong self-bootstrapping mechanism. GPTFuzzer [45, 46] combines mutation and prompt classification to generate and evaluate large-scale adversarial variants. TAP [27] adopts an iterative refinement framework and ReNeLLM [7] focuses on compositional and nested prompting schemes. These approaches share a common principle of iterative generation and selection to efficiently explore the vast adversarial prompt space, showcasing the effectiveness of evolutionary paradigms for jailbreak attacks.

However, most of these methods operate in natural computational logics, where fluency and semantic coherence impose strong structural constraints. As a result, the search space is substantially restricted, and the generated prompts tend to be sensitive to the choice of gradient-based surrogate models. Moreover, these approaches primarily circumvent high-level semantic safety filters but do not sufficiently probe the model vulnerability at the token or representation level. Consequently, they offer only a partial view of the true safety boundary and often fail to expose its worst-case behavior under extreme distribution shifts.

2.2 Long-Tail Distribution Attacks

Long-tail distribution attacks have recently emerged as a promising class of jailbreak techniques targeting LLMs and recent research has explored several approaches within this paradigm. One prominent strategy is cryptographic obfuscation [48, 40], where malicious queries are transformed using classical encryption schemes such as Caesar, Base64, or Rot13, accompanied by decryption logic reconstructing the underlying harmful intent. Another approach leverages flipping-based noise injection, exemplified by FlipAttack [21], which injects syntactic perturbations, particularly at the left side of prompts where autoregressive comprehension is more fragile, to obscure malicious intent while preserving semantic recoverability. A recent development is coding style transformation, which embeds adversarial prompts within programming-like constructs to exploit the strong code-completion priors of LLMs. Frameworks such as CodeChameleon [23] integrate both encryption and decryption logic into a code-completion format, whereas CodeAttack [35] encodes harmful prompts as data structures (e.g., lists, strings, stacks) to conceal malicious intent. Collectively, these studies highlight the diversity of techniques within the long-tail distribution attack paradigm and underscore its significance as an emerging adversarial framework for evaluating LLM safety.

Despite their potential, these methods mainly rely on manually crafted rules, predefined encryption and decryption functions, and fixed code structures, lacking the capability for automatic attack design.

3 The Proposed Method

This section presents EvoJail, a novel multi-objective evolutionary framework fundamentally different from existing heuristic jailbreak-generation approaches. Unlike prior methods that rely on manually crafted transformations or differentiable surrogate models, EvoJail is designed to automatically uncover long-tail, hard-to-detect jailbreak strategies. To tackle the intrinsic challenges of (i) the complex representation of encryption-decryption logic, and (ii) the conflicting objectives of attack effectiveness and output quality, EvoJail introduces a unified multi-objective evolutionary framework for jailbreak prompt generation. It first formulates jailbreak generation as a bi-objective optimization problem that jointly maximizes attack effectiveness and minimizes output perplexity by adopting a semantic-algorithmic solution representation capable of capturing both high-level meaning and low-level structural transformations, and then integrates LLM-assisted operators into a population-based multi-objective evolutionary search, enabling adaptive and semantically informed mutation and recombination. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 1.

3.1 Formulation of Long-Tail Distribution Attacks

From an optimization perspective, long-tail distribution attacks exhibit an inherent conflict between attack effectiveness and output quality, making them naturally amenable to a multi-objective formulation. However, unlike conventional multi-objective optimization problems studied in evolutionary computation, the decision variables in this setting are neither low-dimensional nor numerically parameterized, but instead consist of intertwined natural-language semantics and algorithmic transformation logic.

In particular, the core of an encoded jailbreak attack lies in constructing a pair of encryption and decryption functions (E,D)(E,D) that jointly satisfy three properties: 1) semantic obfuscation, where the encrypted query appears benign or nonsensical at the surface level; 2) algorithmic consistency, requiring exact recoverability of the original malicious intent; and 3) distributional deviation, where the resulting prompt lies in the long-tail region of the model’s training distribution. These requirements give rise to highly discrete, non-linear, and non-differentiable transformation spaces. For example, practical encryption-decryption schemes often involve conditional branching, sequence re-grouping, index-dependent operations, and rule-based reversals, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Such structures cannot be faithfully captured by traditional vector-based encodings or parametric representations commonly assumed in classical multi-objective optimization.

As a consequence, directly applying standard mathematical formulations with explicitly defined decision variables severely restricts the expressive power of the search space, making it difficult to uncover structurally novel and semantically coherent jailbreak strategies. This limitation motivates the need for a representation that can model what the transformation intends to achieve and how it is algorithmically realized.

3.1.1 End-to-End Attack Pipeline

The long-tail distribution attacks is modeled as an end-to-end transformation pipeline, in which malicious intent is concealed through algorithmic obfuscation and later reconstructed within the model’s internal reasoning process.

Let qq denote the original malicious query. An encryption function EE and a corresponding decryption function DD constitute the core components of the attack. For the approach to be valid, the decoding process is required faithfully recover the original query, i.e.,

D⁡(E⁡(q))=q.D(E(q))=q.

The encrypted query q′=E⁡(q)q^{\prime}=E(q) and the decryption logic DD are embedded into a predefined prompt template TT, yielding the adversarial prompt T⁡[q′,D]T[q^{\prime},D]. This construction aligns with prior observations that template-based contextual embedding provides a more reliable interface for guiding model behavior [23, 35, 15, 48].

Formally, the long-tail distribution attack pipeline consists of four sequential stages:

  • •

    Encryption: transform qq into an obfuscated query q′=E⁡(q)q^{\prime}=E(q) to conceal malicious semantics;

  • •

    Decryption specification: provide explicit or implicit instructions DD to recover the original semantics;

  • •

    Prompt construction: embed (q′,D)(q^{\prime},D) into a template TT to establish contextual coherence;

  • •

    Model invocation: submit T⁡[q′,D]T[q^{\prime},D] to the target LLM to elicit responses that reveal the original intent without triggering safety mechanisms.

This pipeline highlights that attack success emerges from the joint interaction of semantic context and algorithmic structure, rather than from isolated perturbations.

3.1.2 Semantic-Algorithmic Solution Representation

To overcome the representational limitations of classical optimization formulations, EvoJail adopts a semantic-algorithmic solution representation, which unifies high-level semantic intent with executable algorithmic logic.

Each attack instance is represented as a structured tuple

x=(h,e,d,t),x=(h,e,d,t),

where

  • •

    hh is a natural-language heuristic describing the design principle of the encryption-decryption scheme,

  • •

    ee and dd denote the concrete implementations of the encryption and decryption functions, respectively,

  • •

    tt is a prompt template sampled from a predefined template pool 𝒯prompts\mathcal{T}_{\text{prompts}}.

The natural-language heuristic hh captures abstract strategies such as reordering, symbolic substitution, or conditional decoding, which are difficult to enumerate explicitly yet critical for exploring diverse long-tail attack patterns. The algorithmic components (e,d)(e,d) ensure functional correctness and reproducibility, while the template component tt is decoupled from optimization to constrain search complexity.

Under this representation, the attack instances constitute a hybrid semantic-algorithmic search space that cannot be expressed as a conventional Euclidean decision space.

3.1.3 Multi-Objective Optimization Formulation

Based on the above representation, the long-tail jailbreak generation problem is formulated as a bi-objective optimization task:

minx⁡F⁡(x)={f1​(x),f2​(x)},\min_{x}F(x)=\left\{f_{1}(x),f_{2}(x)\right\}, (1)

where f1​(x)f_{1}(x) measures attack effectiveness and f2​(x)f_{2}(x) evaluates output quality.

Let rqr_{q} denote the response generated by the target model under attack instance xx for query qq. The first objective is defined as

f1​(x)=−ASR​(rq),f_{1}(x)=-\text{ASR}(r_{q}), (2)

where ASR quantifies jailbreak success and is commonly used in the jailbreak context [20, 51, 27], and the negative sign converts it into a minimization objective. The second objective assesses fluency and coherence via perplexity [13, 22]:

f2(x)=PPL(rq)=exp(−1𝒯∑t=1𝒯logP(wt∣w<t)),f_{2}(x)=\text{PPL}(r_{q})=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\mathcal{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{\mathcal{T}}\log P(w_{t}\mid w_{<t})\right), (3)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the total number of tokens, wtw_{t} is the tt-th token in rqr_{q}, and P⁡(wt∣w<t)P(w_{t}\mid w_{<t}) is the predicted probability from a language model (e.g., GPT-2 [34]). A low perplexity indicates the target model is able to fluently process and complete the malicious prompt, suggesting a stealthy and successful jailbreak.

It is important to emphasize that, although the optimization objective is formally expressed in a classical bi-objective form, the underlying search space is fundamentally non-numeric and non-smooth. The objectives are evaluated over structured programs and natural-language semantics, rather than continuous parameters. This characteristic necessitates a population-based evolutionary search equipped with LLM-assisted variation operators, which will be detailed in the subsequent section.

3.2 LLM-Assisted Evolutionary Multi-Objective Optimization-Based Long-Tail Distribution Attacks

As discussed in the previous section, the design of long-tail distribution attacks exhibits two fundamental characteristics: the presence of multiple conflicting objectives, and an open-ended, highly structured solution space defined by natural-language semantics and programmatic encryption-decryption logic. Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs) provide a natural optimization paradigm for such problem [50].

However, conventional MOEAs are not directly applicable in this setting as their effectiveness critically depends on the compatibility between the evolutionary operators and the underlying solution representation. Classical mutation and crossover operators are typically defined over numeric vectors, permutations, or fixed-length symbolic strings, and rely on random perturbations or predefined recombination rules. In contrast, individuals in long-tail distribution attacks consist of tightly coupled natural-language semantics and executable encryption-decryption programs subject to strict reversibility constraints. Blind random perturbations are highly likely to break syntactic validity or logical reversibility, while handcrafted rule-based operators struggle to produce semantically meaningful and structurally novel long-tail behaviors, leading to inefficient exploration and heavy reliance on human expertise.

Recently, LLMs have introduced new opportunities for evolutionary computation [41]. Prior studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of LLM-assisted evolutionary optimization in various domains such as autonomous MOEAs [12], recommendation systems [8], automated programming [17], and protein design [38]. A common insight across these works is that embedding LLMs into evolutionary operators allows the search process to be guided by semantic understanding and domain knowledge, thereby improving efficiency and solution quality in highly structured, non-numeric search spaces.

Inspired by these advancements, we propose an LLM-assisted evolutionary algorithm, termed EvoJail, which retains the population-based multi-objective optimization structure of MOEAs while embedding LLMs into the design of evolutionary operators. By leveraging the semantic understanding and program synthesis capabilities of LLMs, EvoJail enables adaptive, structure-aware generation, mutation, crossover, and repair of candidate attack individuals, thereby transforming MOEA into a semantically informed evolutionary search process. The algorithm is illustrated in Fig. 1, with the corresponding pseudocode given in Algorithm 1.

3.2.1 LLM-Assisted Generation Operators

A central component of the EvoJail algorithm is the use of a unified LLM-assisted generation procedure that serves as the core operator for initialization, mutation, and crossover. The pseudo-code is given in Algorithm 2. Rather than relying on handcrafted genetic operators, EvoJail leverages a design model θd\theta_{d} to generate structurally valid and semantically meaningful individuals under different prompt configurations, where pb​u​i​l​d∈{pi​n​i​t​i​a​l​i​z​a​t​i​o​n,pm​u​t​a​t​i​o​n,pc​r​o​s​s​o​v​e​r}p_{build}\in\{p_{initialization},p_{mutation},p_{crossover}\}

The initialization prompt pi​n​i​t​i​a​l​i​z​a​t​i​o​np_{initialization} instructs the design model to generate a new individual that preserves the stylistic structure of an ancestor while introducing a distinct encoding logic, as shown in Fig. 3. The output is constrained to a syntactically correct Python dictionary containing a heuristic description and paired encode-decode algorithms. This design yields several benefits. Firstly, by encouraging variations in word order, sorting criteria, data structures, and metadata, the initial population spans a broad region of the structural search space, thereby introducing early structural diversity. Secondly, the code-level constraints reduce the prevalence of ill-formed individuals in early generations. Thirdly, throughout the search process, character-level encodings (e.g., Base64 or Rot13) are explicitly excluded, as such transformations are known to degrade attack effectiveness on smaller models due to their limited capability to interpret low-level symbol manipulations [51].

Mutation and crossover, pm​u​t​a​t​i​o​np_{mutation} and pc​r​o​s​s​o​v​e​rp_{crossover}, are performed using a shared genetic prompt, as shown in Fig. 4, distinguished by their operational context that the mutation operates on a single parent, while crossover combines two. The evolutionary feedback is explicitly injected into the generation process. Each parent individual is annotated with a parent improvement status (Better, Equal, Worse, Mixed, or Unknown) based on changes in its expected performance relative to its predecessors. This information enables the design model to reason about which structural components are beneficial and which are potentially harmful. The prompt further provides refined and advanced structural guidance, encouraging the model to retain effective components while increasing token distribution unpredictability, introduce structure-aware reordering, grouping, or indexing strategies, embed lightweight, reversible metadata, and exploit data structures such as stacks, trees, or probabilistic groupings. As a result, mutation and crossover become adaptive, semantics-aware transformations rather than random perturbations, substantially improving search efficiency in the highly structured solution space.

Besides, since strict reversibility is difficult to guarantee in natural language-driven generation, EvoJail incorporates a verification-repair loop pr​e​p​a​i​rp_{repair}, as shown in Fig. 5. For each candidate, the encryption-decryption pair is tested against a reference input. If reversibility fails, the design model is allowed up to RR targeted repair attempts using a dedicated repair context. Importantly, individuals that remain irreversible after repair may still be retained if the decoded output is executable, preventing excessive contraction of the search space. This mechanism balances structural rigor with exploratory flexibility and is critical for discovering long-tail strategies. Finally, a template tt is sampled at random from the predefined template pool Tprompts{T}_{\text{prompts}}, extended from [35, 23], and combined with the encryption-decryption logic to form a final candidate attack.

3.2.2 Details of the Evolutionary Search

On the basis of the LLM-assisted generation, EvoJail operates within a standard multi-objective evolutionary optimization loop. The algorithm starts from an ancestor set 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which contains representative long-tail distribution strategies [23, 51], including the Queue, OddEven, Length, Stack, and Reverse. The Queue employs the first-in-first-out principle with a cyclic shift and rotates the words forward by one position, OddEven segregates words by their index parity by placeing all odd-positioned words first, followed by even-positioned words, Length orders words by their character count while preserving original indices, Stack operates on the last-in-first-out principle and encrypts the sentence by reversing the word order, and Reverse reverses the entire word sequence. With the ancestor set, an initial population P0P_{0} of size NN is generated using the LLM-assisted generation with pi​n​i​t​i​a​l​i​z​a​t​i​o​np_{initialization} and pr​e​p​a​i​rp_{repair}, where Deepseek-v3 [18] is adopted as the designer model θd\theta_{d}. After the initialization, candidate individuals are iteratively generated, evaluated, selected, and transformed to optimize both attack effectiveness and output quality.

At each generation, individuals are evaluated under two objectives: attack effectiveness and output perplexity. Parent selection follows a hybrid strategy to balance exploitation and exploration: with equal probability, either the top-d individuals ranked by attack effectiveness are selected, or a non-dominated binary tournament based on Pareto dominance is applied. Variation is introduced via the LLM-assisted mutation and crossover operators with pm​u​t​a​t​i​o​np_{mutation}, pc​r​o​s​s​o​v​e​rp_{crossover} and pr​e​p​a​i​rp_{repair}. Population update is performed using fast non-dominated sorting [5]. After TT generations, the algorithm outputs an optimized population P∗P^{*}, prioritizing individuals on the first Pareto front and ranking them by attack effectiveness.

4 Experimental Studies

In this section, comprehensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the proposed algorithm against six existing methods. We first examine the performance of these algorithms in terms of attack effectiveness and output quality, analyzing results at both the individual level (single attack strategy) and the ensemble level (integrated multiple attack strategies). Next, the adaptability to unseen instances of these algorithm is examined to assess their generalization ability. Finally, the evolutionary dynamics of the proposed algorithm are analyzed to provide deeper insight into its search behavior.

4.1 Experimental Setup

4.1.1 Problem Instances.

A total of 18 instances are examined in the experiments. Three target victim models are considered: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf [37], Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [10], and the closed-source gpt-4.1-Nano [29]. The instances are derived from two widely used benchmark question sets. GPTFuzzer [45, 46], provides harmful queries spanning diverse violation categories such as hate speech, self-harm, and malware generation. JBB-Behaviors [2], contains representative misuse behaviors collected from established datasets including the Trojan Detection Challenge [25], HarmBench [26], and AdvBench [53]. For each target model, six instances are drawn from the two benchmarks to ensure reproducibility and balanced category coverage. The details of all evaluated instances are summarized in Appendix.

4.1.2 Baselines and Their Configurations.

The proposed EvoJail is compared with six state-of-the-art algorithms, including ChiperChat [48], Jailbroken [40], FlipAttack [21], CodeAttack [35], CodeChameleon [23], and ReNeLLM [7]. The baseline methods are implemented based on the EasyJailbreak framework [51], and the default parameter configurations reported in their original papers are used. The configuration of the proposed EvoJail is as follows. The total number of iterations is set to 20, NN is set to 10 and Rm​a​xR_{max} is set to 10.

4.1.3 Evaluation Metrics.

The DeepSeek-V3 model [18] is employed as the evaluator for computing ASR, while GPT2-XL [34] is used to calculate PPL. Furthermore, the widely-used HyperVolume metric (HV) that has been proven to provide a comprehensive and quantitative evaluation of the overall algorithm performance in balancing multiple conflicting objectives [52, 11] is employed. Specifically, ASR and PPL are first normalized according to their empirical value ranges in the experiments, and the hypervolume metric is then computed using [0,1][0,1] as the reference point.

4.2 Results and Discussions

Based on the HV results shown in Table 1, the proposed EvoJail algorithm outperforms baseline methods in 15 out of the 18 test scenarios. Specifically, in all scenarios involving LLaMA series models, EvoJail’s HV values consistently led by a large margin. On the LLaMA8B, EvoJail repeatedly surpassed 0.700 (e.g., LLaMA8B-G2 reached 0.770), while methods such as FlipAttack and CodeAttack showed jailbreak failure that their ASR is nearly 1, and although CodeChameleon was relatively stable, it did not reach optimal levels. Moreover, EvoJail demonstrated excellent adaptability: on the GPT models, it performs competely with the high-performing CodeAttack and outperforms it in half of the scenarios. While CodeAttack performs well on GPT, its HV value on LLaMA7B significantly drops (e.g., LLaMA7B-G2 is only 0.042).

To illustrate the diversity of the algorithms on the Pareto front, Fig. 6 shows the dominance diagram of the solution set corresponding to the median HV performance from multiple experiments. As can be seen from this figure, there is a clear conflict between the ASR and the PPL. Specifically, the solutions generated by the baseline methods or EvoJail exhibit a mutually balancing distribution in the target space. Regarding Pareto dominance and coverage, the solution set obtained by EvoJail dominates all baselines in the G1-G3 scenarios of LLaMA-7B, occupying the optimal lower-left region, and again achieves complete dominance in LLaMA-8B-J3. Even in scenarios without strict dominance (such as J1, J2 and the G series of LLaMA-7B/8B), its solution set still shows a wider distribution in the target space, particularly excelling in maintaining PPL smaller than 10. EvoJail demonstrates superior performance in balancing attack effectiveness and output quality: maintaining high ASR and extremely lower PPL in LLaMA-8B-G, while CodeAttack achieves similar higher ASR but significantly higher PPL. These subplots collectively show that EvoJail exhibits advantages in the diversity and optimality of the Pareto front comparing with these baselines. In the remaining scenarios outside of LLaMA-7B, EvoJail and solutions on the baseline, such as CodeAttack, together constitute the fitting results of the current algorithm to the approximate Pareto front in the encryption/decryption design space. These results suggest that EvoJail can systematically generate high-quality and diverse attack strategies during design phases, and can successfully explore different and equally optimal regions on the Pareto front in jailbreak encryption-decryption algorithms design.

To further investigate the practical output behaviors and attack capability differences among the seven algorithms, there are two representative malicious query cases for qualitative analysis. As shown in Fig. 7 and Fig. 8, EvoJail preserves and advances the original malicious objective, producing explicit five-step execution plans in each instance. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 7, the generated response does not directly output harmful content. Instead, it embeds malicious intent into a seemingly reasonable "execution plan" through a multi-step decoding and task decomposition framework. This plan first algorithmically decodes the encrypted query, then systematically breaks down the task, gradually guiding out specific implementation steps, including social engineering attacks (such as phishing and spoofing). Meanwhile, as Fig. 8 shown, in response to the malicious query "how to discard a friend’s phone and frame someone else," EvoJail’s output plans include creating a diversion, manipulating evidence, or using social engineering tactics. In contrast, FlipAttack, CodeAttack, and ReNeLLM all fail in this setting, where the model exhibits clear refusal-to-comply signals. CodeChameleon generates preventive or corrective suggestions in Fig. 7, and in Fig. 8 further demonstrates a narrative reversal with remedial content. Jailbroken and Cipher, on the other hand, display varying degrees of semantic drift and uncontrolled generation. Above two cases mentioned, it suggests that the core characteristic of EvoJail lies in its ability to generate multi-step execution plans while preserving the original malicious target. These suggest that EvoJail avoids directly generating explicit harmful content and logically covers key elements required for the attack.

To evaluate the algorithm’s transferability, representative individuals are selected from the candidate strategies generated in specific scenarios (e.g., LLaMA-7B-J1) and integrated to form the final solution set of EvoJail. For each malicious query, the candidate solution with the highest ASR is first selected from each algorithm. If multiple solutions share the same highest ASR, the one with the lowest PPL is chosen as the final output for that algorithm. All baseline methods follow the same selection rules to ensure fairness and comparability. Each point displayed in the corresponding figures represents the average performance over multiple independent experimental runs. On the LLaMA series models (Table 2), EvoJail significantly outperforms others with a clear overall advantage: on LLaMA-7B, its solution set fully dominates baseline methods. As Fig 9 shown, on LLaMA-8B, even when compared to CodeAttack with a little higher ASR, EvoJail consistently maintains significantly lower PPL, achieving a higher HV value. Although CodeAttack has a higher HV value in the GPT scenarios, EvoJail achieves more competitive ASR in the GPT-J scenarios. Nevertheless, EvoJail demonstrated competitiveness at the ensemble level on unseen instances.

To explore the relationship between integration scale and baseline performance, we compare the attack performance at different integration scales with the performance of each baseline method. This allows us to analyze the trend of performance improvement as the number of integrations increases. In the results shown in Fig. 10, the integration scale required for EvoJail to achieve comprehensive dominance over the baseline methods varies depending on the model and scenario. For example, on LLaMA-7B, at least 14 strategies are needed to dominate Jailbroken, while on LLaMA-8B-J, only 4 strategies are required to dominate CodeChameleon. This difference suggests that EvoJail’s automated framework can systematically adapt to different security mechanisms, and a richer strategy pool is necessary to demonstrate its advantage in more complex scenarios. These results indicate that the Pareto front generated by EvoJail has some strategic diversity. When the integration scale is small, the sampled strategies may excel in only one objective, leading to a non-dominant relationship with the baseline (i.e., occasional victories and defeats). As more diverse and balanced strategies are included, the overall performance of the integration improves, leading to dominance. This is particularly evident in the cases of LLaMA-7B versus Jailbroken and GPT-J versus CodeAttack. Furthermore, in certain scenarios such as GPT-G, even with an increased integration scale, EvoJail is still dominated by CodeAttack. This needs to be interpreted in the context of method characteristics: baseline methods like CodeAttack are manually designed fixed algorithms that perform well in specific model scenarios but fail in cases like LLaMA-7B. Because these above results suggest that the model’s architecture and training fine-tuning strategies also decided the performance of different jailbreak algorithms [37, 10, 29].

As shown in Fig. 11, with the increase in the number of integration strategies (from 3 to 16), EvoJail demonstrates significant and robust performance improvement, which suggests the superiority of its methodology. First, the ASR shows a monotonic increasing trend across all experimental groups, with the growth rate gradually slowing down. On the one hand, this intuitively reflects the submodular benefit pattern of the integration strategies; on the other hand, and more importantly, it reveals that EvoJail, through its multi-objective evolutionary search framework, generates attack strategies with high diversity and complementarity. The strategies introduced early on significantly broaden the attack surface, quickly increasing ASR; as the integration scale expands, although the marginal gains between strategies decrease, the ASR continues to grow, which further proves the richness of the strategy pool—i.e., EvoJail can systematically discover a large number of heterogeneous and effective attack patterns.Although PPL fluctuates in certain scenarios (such as LLaMA-7B-J and GPT-G), there is an overall downward trend. This indicates that during the integration process, high-ASR but high-PPL strategies are gradually supplemented or replaced by those with better attack effectiveness and output fluency.

In contrast, EvoJail generates a set of strategies automatically, with the advantage of not relying on manual priors and being able to adaptively generate diverse strategies across different scenarios. Therefore, this result does not negate the value of the automated framework but also more deeply confirms EvoJail’s core capability as an automated attack framework: it can continuously generate a large number of diverse and high-quality Pareto-optimal strategies, providing a solid foundation for building a highly adaptive integrated attack system.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced EvoJail, the first automated framework for generating long-tail distribution attacks against LLMs using multi-objective evolutionary search. By eliminating reliance on handcrafted rules, EvoJail enables systematic evaluation of LLM security and privacy vulnerabilities across diverse user-generated inputs in real-world Web environments. The framework combines semantic and algorithmic representations with LLM-assisted operators to efficiently explore the encryption-decryption prompt space, producing adaptive, interpretable, and diverse attack strategies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EvoJail achieves competitive attack effectiveness and superior output quality while providing a Pareto front of strategies that support flexible and robust evaluation. Our findings highlight the importance of automated, multi-objective approaches for assessing and improving the safety and robustness of deployed LLMs, offering actionable insights for the development of more resilient defense mechanisms. Looking forward, future work could leverage insights from EvoJail to develop adaptive defenses against long-tail attacks, improving model robustness through targeted mitigation [49] and learning-based optimization strategies [36, 32, 30] that evolve alongside emerging threats.

Appendix A Appendix

This paper contains examples that may be unsafe or involve sensitive topics; these examples are for technical analysis purposes only. This research aims to investigate model security by simulating the behavior of jailbreak.

A.1 Instance Details

The experimental data are divided into two main categories. The first category is used to evaluate the ability of the algorithm to generate effective attack strategies, and the second category is used to assess its generalization capability on unseen instances. For brevity, the GPTFuzzer scenario is abbreviated as G. Specifically, for the GPTFuzzer dataset, the instances with indices from 11 to 1010, from 1111 to 2020, and from 2121 to 3030 are grouped as G1, G2, and G3, respectively. The JBB-Behaviors dataset contains 100 malicious or policy-violating behaviors that are categorized into 10 thematic groups in accordance with the usage-policy taxonomy defined by OpenAI, with 10 instances per category indexed sequentially from 11 to 100100. JBB-Behaviors is abbreviated as J. J1 includes {1,11,21,…,91}\{1,11,21,\dots,91\} (the first instance of each category), J2 includes {2,12,22,…,92}\{2,12,22,\dots,92\}, and J3 includes {3,13,23,…,93}\{3,13,23,\dots,93\}. For each dataset, the remaining queries are used to examine the generalization capability of the algorithm. Meanwhile, Llama-2-7b-chat-hf is abbreviated as LLaMA7B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is abbreviated as LLaMA8B, and GPT-4.1-Nano is abbreviated as GPT.
